---
title: "Group Work"
---

> In this group project, you will work in a group of 2–3 participants to develop and analyze a realistic business analytics case.
> The project focuses on business-relevant contexts such as management, finance, operations, or digital platforms and should be grounded in appropriate and reputable references, such as academic literature and industry reports.
> You will formulate a concrete business problem and design a synthetic dataset that reflects a realistic organizational process or decision situation.
> You will then apply appropriate machine learning methods to analyze the data and address the business problem.
> This allows you to engage with both upstream challenges—such as problem framing and data design—and downstream challenges such as deployment, implementation, ethics, and risk.

## Objectives

- Design a realistic business analytics scenario
- Select and apply appropriate machine learning methods
- Communicate results using CRISP-DM as a structuring framework
- Critically reflect on assumptions, limitations, and improvements

## Group formation and topic proposal

- Form your own group of **2–3 participants**.
- One member of the group must send an **email to [{{< meta instructor.email >}}](mailto:{{< meta instructor.email >}}) by {{< meta group_work.proposal_deadline >}}** containing:

  - the names of all group members;
  - a concise proposed project topic; and
  - the concrete business or analytical question the group intends to address.

- Proposed topics will be reviewed during the following week.
  The instructor may request adjustments if topics overlap too strongly or the proposed scope is unsuitable.

## Project topics

The following are **illustrative examples**, not predefined project options:

- **Finance**, such as credit default, fraud, or customer lifetime value
- **Marketing**, such as churn, customer segmentation, or campaign response
- **Human Resources**, such as attrition, promotion, or team productivity
- **Digital Business**, such as user engagement, gig worker retention, or demand prediction

Propose a concrete business problem and analytical question rather than merely selecting a generic domain.

## Task

- Define a practical business problem or decision situation and formulate a concrete analytical question.
- Create a synthetic but realistic dataset representing internal organizational data.
  You may complement this with synthetic or real external data if appropriate.
  Generate the synthetic data reproducibly in a separate R script.
- Develop an integrated Quarto analysis document (`.qmd`) containing the explanation of the business context, R code, executed results, and figures or tables.
  It must present the complete, reproducible analysis following CRISP-DM.
- Present and critically reflect on what can be learned from the case, its connection to course content, simplifying assumptions and limitations, and opportunities for improvement.
- Complete an advanced extension.
  This is the primary area in which your project should differ from a straightforward reproduction of techniques practiced in class.
  Possible extensions include an analytical technique or methodological refinement beyond classroom examples; more sophisticated or realistic data preparation; model comparison or refinement; robustness or sensitivity analysis; a realistic complication in the business setting; deployment or implementation considerations; organizational or decision-process implications; ethical, fairness, governance, or risk considerations; or interactive or otherwise improved communication of results.
  The extension does not have to use a more complex machine-learning algorithm.
  A realistic and thoughtful extension involving deployment, robustness, ethics, or the business process can satisfy this requirement.

::: {.callout-note title="Notes"}

- Support key elements of your analysis with reputable sources, particularly the relevance of the problem, typical data sources, and common modeling approaches.
- Simplifications are acceptable and can be valuable if they are clearly stated and justified. Use the report to explain how a more realistic analysis could extend beyond these simplifications.
- Your code must run from the submitted files and reproduce the reported results.
- If you plan to work with a large-scale big-data scenario, consult with me in advance.
- Real-time or streaming-data projects require careful consideration of their additional technical complexity and whether they can be meaningfully implemented and evaluated within the scope of the project.

:::

## Project process

### Proposal and review

Form your group and email the group details, proposed topic, and concrete question by **{{< meta group_work.proposal_deadline >}}**.
Topics will be reviewed during the following week, and substantial overlap or unsuitable scope will be resolved with the affected groups.

### Project work

Develop the case, dataset, analysis, required advanced extension, and presentation iteratively.
Your work should progress from problem framing and dataset design to analysis, modeling, evaluation, and reflection.

If questions come up during the project phase, you can arrange a meeting:

- Book appointments via: [Bookings]({{< meta instructor.bookings_url >}})
- Join meetings via: [Teams]({{< meta instructor.online_meeting_url >}})

### Presentation

- Available group-presentation dates: **{{< meta group_work.presentation_dates_display >}}**.
- Each group will receive an individual presentation slot after groups and topics have been finalized.
- Each group has **30 minutes** to present the project.
- Up to **15 additional minutes** may be used for questions and discussion.
- Every group member must present part of the project and contribute to the discussion.
- Attendance is required for all project presentations.
- **All groups** must submit their presentation material and the relevant analysis files by **{{< meta group_work.presentation_submission_deadline >}}**, irrespective of their own assigned presentation slot.
- Presentation submission channel: **{{< meta group_work.presentation_submission_channel >}}**.

### Final submission

- Final submission deadline: **{{< meta group_work.submission_date >}}**.
- Submit via the [Canvas assignment]({{< meta group_work.submission_url >}}).
- Submit the Quarto source file (`.qmd`), the completed rendered PDF, data files, and R script for generating the synthetic dataset.

{{< pagebreak >}}

## Deliverables

### Presentation

Submit the presentation as a PDF. The presentation should:

- Clearly introduce the business problem and decision context
- Explain the analytical approach and key modeling decisions
- Communicate the most important findings and their practical relevance
- Critically discuss limitations, risks, the required advanced extension, and potential improvements

### Synthetic dataset and generation script

Submit the **R script used to generate the synthetic dataset** together with the resulting **dataset file(s)**, normally as CSV files.
The generation script should document the business purpose, schema, generation logic, assumptions, distributions, relationships, and realism features such as noise or missing values where appropriate.
Use a fixed random seed so that the dataset can be reproduced from the script.
Keep the generation logic in a separate R script rather than embedding it in the main `.qmd`.

### Main report

Submit your analysis as a Quarto document (.qmd) together with its rendered PDF.

The `.qmd` is the central analytical artifact and integrates the report and analytical work in one narrative.
It must contain the full CRISP-DM analysis, explanatory text, R code, executed results, and the figures and tables needed to support the argument.
Do not create a second, redundant report narrative.

The **main report text is limited to 12 pages**.
The title page, references, and appendices are excluded from this limit; appendices may provide supporting detail but must not be used to evade the limit.
Include enough code and results to make the work reproducible while keeping the prose focused.

To create the submitted PDF, give the document a PDF format in its YAML header (for example, `format: pdf`) and run:

```bash
quarto render your-analysis.qmd --to pdf
```

Rendering must execute the R code (do not disable execution or rely on stale results).
Check that the generated PDF contains the completed analysis and all results.
Submit **both** the `.qmd` source and this rendered `.pdf`; the submitted source, data, and supporting files must reproduce the PDF.

## Individual contributions

Each student must identify approximately **three pages of report text** for which they were the primary author.
Thus, in a three-person group with a 12-page report, approximately three pages per student should be individually attributed.

Include a brief contribution statement at the end of the report indicating which sections or subsections were primarily written by each group member.
Not every section needs to be assigned to a single person: some parts may be written jointly or developed through contributions from several group members.
The contribution statement should provide transparent evidence of each member’s meaningful written contribution without implying that assigned sections were produced entirely independently.

Every group member must also make a meaningful contribution to the analysis, presentation, and discussion.

{{< pagebreak >}}

## Evaluation

The final group evaluation is **primarily based on the submitted project materials and is worth 120 performance points**.

The presentation is a **mandatory formative milestone** rather than a separately graded component. Use the presentation and subsequent discussion to test your argument, identify weaknesses, and obtain feedback that should inform and improve the final report.

Participation in the presentation and discussion may additionally be considered when assessing individual contributions.

::: {.small}

| Category | Points | Criteria |
|---------|---:|------------------|
| **A. Case and dataset design** | 30 pts | Clarity and relevance of the problem; realism of the dataset; transparency of data generation |
| **B. Analysis quality** | 40 pts | Method justification; correctness; CRISP-DM use; insightfulness |
| **C. Communication** | 40 pts | Structure; visualization; clean code; argument quality; use of references; reflection |
| **D. Advanced extension** | 10 pts | Meaningful differentiation beyond straightforward reproduction of classroom examples |

:::

### AI policy

- Allowed: debugging code and to create the R script for synthetic dataset creation
- Not allowed: generating complete end-to-end solutions
- You must be able to explain and defend your work at any time
- All outputs must be validated

{{< pagebreak >}}

## Example: Synthetic data generation in R

```{r}
#| eval: false

set.seed(42)
n <- 1000

# Generate related variables and add realistic noise.
age <- rnorm(n, mean = 40, sd = 10)
income <- age * 1000 + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 5000)

# Add missing values where they are appropriate to the scenario.
income[runif(n) < 0.05] <- NA_real_

dataset <- data.frame(age, income)
write.csv(dataset, "dataset.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

Adapt and document the generation logic for your own business context.

High-quality project work may contribute to future course development, for example by extending teaching materials or informing teaching cases.
In such cases, we will discuss how contributions are acknowledged.
:::
